name: Hoop house
seoDesc: Hoop house: work out height of sidewalls (H₁) (Greenhouse details) from the total height (H₁ + H₂) and the slant height. A free construction calculator…
summary: Give the Hoop house calculator the total height (H₁ + H₂), the slant height and the total width and it returns height of sidewalls (H₁) (Greenhouse details). Think of it as a shortcut for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Hoop house calculator work?
sections.html:
The Hoop house calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports height of sidewalls (H₁) (Greenhouse details) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the greenhouse type and the material); then you type in the total height (H₁ + H₂) (Greenhouse details), the slant height (Greenhouse details), the slant height (Greenhouse details) and the total width (W).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Hoop house calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Height of sidewalls (H₁)=-gable height (H₂) + total height (H₁ + H₂)
Gable height (H₂)=(1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (4 × (slant height ^ 2) − (total width (W) ^ 2))
Length (L)=(-1 ÷ 2 × gable height (H₂) × total width (W) − height of sidewalls (H₁) × total width (W) + (1 ÷ 2) × surface Area) ÷ (height of sidewalls (H₁) + slant height)
Width (W)=(1 ÷ 6) × (3 × bow length − 4 × PI × height (H) + the square root of (3 × (bow length ^ 2) + 12 × PI × bow length × height (H) − 20 × (PI ^ 2) × (height (H) ^ 2))) ÷ PI
Bow length=2 × (-PI × height (H) × width (W) + surface Area) ÷ length (L)
Total height (H)=the square root of ((slant height − width (W)) × (slant height + width (W)))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Hoop house calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the total height (H₁ + H₂), the slant height and the total width — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Hoop house calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns height of sidewalls (H₁) (Greenhouse details), derived from the total height (H₁ + H₂), the slant height and the total width. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Hoop house calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the total height (H₁ + H₂), the slant height and the total width, which is 22 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter total height (H₁ + H₂) (Greenhouse details) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Total height (H₁ + H₂) (Greenhouse details) opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Heat loss coefficient = 0 W/(m²·K). Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Hoop house calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
